claims.text: Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti is a superconducting high-entropy alloy.
The starting alloy has a chemically disordered body-centered-cubic structure.
The alloy has established superconducting properties at ambient pressure.
Hydrostatic pressure will be varied from ambient pressure to approximately 50 GPa while the alloy is cooled below 10 K.
In situ high-pressure XRD will be used to monitor lattice parameters and phase stability.
Pressure reduces the lattice spacing of the alloy.
Pressure changes the alloy's phonon modes or phonon spectrum.
The bcc structure can remain stable throughout the proposed 0–50 GPa pressure interval.
Pressure-induced lattice and phonon changes modify the electron-phonon coupling strength.
An optimal pressure window optimizes electron-phonon coupling.
Optimized electron-phonon coupling strengthens Cooper pairing.
Pressure can increase the superconducting transition temperature of this alloy relative to ambient pressure.
The ambient-pressure transition temperature is approximately 7–8 K.
The transition temperature may reach approximately 10 K.
The optimal pressure range may be approximately 40–60 GPa.
Pressure will produce a sharper, more well-defined superconducting transition than at ambient pressure.
Zero-resistance superconductivity in this alloy is robust over at least the proposed 0–50 GPa interval.
The proposed phonon-tuning interpretation is limited to pressures at which no structural phase transition or major lattice instability occurs.
Resistance, magnetic susceptibility, and XRD will be compared across pressure increments against the ambient-pressure baseline.
A correlation between a change in Tc and a structural phase transition is designated as falsifying the pressure-induced phonon-tuning hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The proposed experiment and stated validity range stop at approximately 50 GPa, while the proposed optimal window extends to 60 GPa; the upper part of that prediction cannot be tested within the stated range.

The boundary excludes structural phase-transition conditions from the hypothesis's intended domain, but the falsification rule treats observation of such a transition as falsification rather than as an out-of-domain result.
